A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same scaling-law study of global weather models. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

before.justification: Section 3 reports original ERA5 training and forecasting experiments across five models. Appendix E also reports ensemble forecasting and CRPS results.

after.justification: V2 retains the original forecasting experiments and CRPS results, and additionally reports hyperparameter-sweep outcomes and synthetic-input throughput measurements.

M1.justification: The five model architectures, scaling-analysis framework, and forecasting procedures are retained. Newly documented optimizer settings do not establish a method revision; µP is evaluated as an alternative during tuning rather than adopted as a new component.

E1.justification: ERA5 coverage and the six-hour global forecasting task remain unchanged. V2 adds a synthetic-input throughput scenario for SFNO and Pangu in Section 4, footnote 1, extending the input conditions used for computational evaluation.

E2.justification: The five-model forecasting comparison and CRPS comparators are retained. Appendix B.2 adds a training-strategy comparison: AIFS with µP-adjusted learning-rate scaling is evaluated against the original scaling approach and reported to have worse validation-loss curves.

E3.justification: Figure 1 changes its highlighted compute-budget comparison from 25 to 100 Pflop. V2 also introduces evaluation conditions for the reported µP trial and synthetic-input throughput checks. The existing ERA5 splits, spatial resolution, and forecast lead remain unchanged; newly disclosed final hyperparameters do not establish reruns.

E4.justification: Appendix B.2 adds qualitative learning-rate and batch-size sensitivity findings, including unstable GraphCast/SFNO settings and unsuccessful µP transfer to AIFS. Section 4 adds synthetic-input checks addressing data-loading bottlenecks. Existing width–depth and ensemble-size analyses are retained.

E5.justification: No repeated-training-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests are added. The existing comparison of 10- and 50-member ensembles and its CRPS reporting are retained in Appendix E of v1 and Appendix F of v2.

E6.justification: Table 2 revises GraphCast’s reported throughput from 0.172 to 10.15 Tflop/s and utilization from 0.017% to 1.03%, moving it from last to third. Aurora’s reported utilization advantage consequently falls from approximately 2000× to 36×, substantially changing the hardware comparison. V2 adds synthetic-input peaks of 9.56 Tflop/s for SFNO and 33.5 Tflop/s for Pangu, plus tuning outcomes. Forecasting results in Figures 2–7 remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The scaling relationships, parameter-count formula, compute-accounting derivations, and loss/CRPS equations are retained. Relabeling Equation (1) as validation rather than training loss corrects its description without changing the mathematics; the new weight tables specify existing quantities.

C1.justification: The main contributions concerning cross-model scaling, width preference, and training-data allocation remain intact. The conclusion narrows its specific hardware-efficiency claim from approximately 2000× to 36× higher utilization for Aurora relative to GraphCast.

C2.justification: V2 newly attributes SFNO and Pangu throughput limitations primarily to data loading. Appendix B.2 discusses the computational limits of exhaustive tuning and argues that language-model tuning heuristics may not transfer directly to continuous weather prediction. Existing architectural interpretations and forecast-scaling limitations remain.

D1.justification: New Appendix B and Table 3 disclose optimizers, learning rates, optimizer betas, batch sizes, parallelization, and tuning ranges across all five models. Appendix D adds explicit variable definitions, units, and numerical loss/inverse-variance weights. Appendix A also identifies the Aurora trainer’s ESFM source. These substantially expand reproducibility information without establishing changes to retained experiments.

R1.justification: V2 adds Yang et al. (2021) for µP and Ozdemir et al. (2026) for the training implementation. Other reference changes largely update or correct existing bibliographic entries. The positioning as a cross-model weather scaling study remains unchanged.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most prose are retained. Local edits clarify the abstract, correct the validation-loss label, and update publication information. Training details are reorganized into a new appendix section, with initialization information moved from the main text.

P2.justification: V2 adds three documentation tables, adjusts Figure 1’s horizontal range and compute markers, clarifies Figure 2’s caption, and reorders Table 2. Existing appendix figures and specification tables are redistributed and renumbered. Most graphical displays retain their original content and design.

improvement.justification: Appendices B and D make the experiments easier to reproduce and audit by supplying previously missing training settings and exact validation weights. The synthetic-input checks also improve the discussion of throughput bottlenecks. These are useful gains, but the main forecasting evidence is unchanged, the tuning evidence remains qualitative, and the large GraphCast throughput revision is unexplained. The net quality improvement is therefore limited.
